mission.title: A journey to the Moon
mission.intro: Three explorers. Two spacecraft. One extraordinary journey.
paragraphs: Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969, carrying Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. Four days later, Armstrong and Aldrin landed in Eagle while Collins orbited above in Columbia.
The landing site was called the Sea of Tranquility. It is a rocky lunar plain, not an ocean of water. The crew returned safely to Earth on July 24.

eagle.title: Meet Eagle
eagle.intro: Two parts, four feet, and a way back home.
paragraphs: Eagle's lower stage carried its landing legs and descent engine. Its upper stage held Armstrong and Aldrin and the engine that would lift them back into lunar orbit.
When the astronauts left, the lower stage stayed on the Moon as a launch platform. Eagle had no wheels. The crew explored on foot.

science.title: Science stayed behind
science.intro: A short visit could begin a much longer scientific story.
paragraphs: The astronauts set out instruments before leaving. A laser reflector returned light toward Earth. A seismometer detected movements of the lunar ground.
These devices had different working lives. The seismic experiment stopped operating in 1969. The passive reflector still supports measurements of the Earth–Moon distance.

reflector.title: A light that comes back
reflector.intro: This instrument does not need batteries to help us measure.
paragraphs: Scientists on Earth aim pulses of laser light at the panel. Its special reflectors send some light back toward the telescope. Timing that journey helps measure the distance to the Moon.
The laser is on Earth. The panel on the Moon reflects it; it does not broadcast a radio message or create its own beam.
reflector.question: Where does the laser light begin its journey?

seismometer.title: Feeling tiny shakes
seismometer.intro: The ground could tell a story, too.
paragraphs: The seismometer measured vibrations of the lunar ground. While Armstrong and Aldrin were still nearby, it detected movements caused by their activities.
It sensed shaking rather than listening to sound in the air. This particular instrument had a short operating life and is no longer transmitting.

photos.title: Eagle at Tranquility Base
photos.intro: An actual photograph from the Apollo 11 moonwalk.
paragraphs: Neil Armstrong photographed Eagle from near Little West Crater. The spacecraft still has both stages in this view; the upper stage had not yet lifted off.
Look for the wide landing feet and the ladder. The complete photograph is shown here, without generated additions.

footprint.title: A footprint with a story
footprint.intro: A familiar photograph deserves its real caption.
paragraphs: Buzz Aldrin photographed this bootprint during the Apollo 11 surface activities. It belongs to his study of the lunar soil, not a photograph of Armstrong taking the first step.
The person who took a picture and the reason it was taken are important parts of its evidence.

samples.title: What came home?
samples.intro: Some discoveries travelled back to Earth.
paragraphs: Armstrong and Aldrin brought back more than 20 kilograms of lunar rocks and soil. These samples gave scientists material to examine in laboratories on Earth.
They also recovered a foil that had collected particles from the solar wind. That foil came home; it was not left as a permanent lunar experiment.

timeline.title: The lunar event record
timeline.intro: One mission, seen in the right order.
paragraphs: Eagle landed on July 20, 1969. Armstrong's first step followed at about 02:56 UTC on July 21. In the eastern United States it was still July 20.
Eagle stayed on the surface for about 22 hours. Its upper stage then carried the two explorers back to meet Collins.

radio.title: Words from the landing
radio.intro: Actual words, with the people and mission times attached.
paragraphs: These short excerpts come from NASA's Apollo Lunar Surface Journal. GET means mission elapsed time: hours, minutes and seconds since launch.
This is a readable transcript selection. No original audio or synthetic voice is being played.

quotes.speaker: Neil Armstrong
quotes.text: Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.

olive.title: A small wish for peace
olive.intro: A small object could carry a very human hope.
paragraphs: The Apollo 11 crew left a small gold replica of an olive branch on the Moon. It represented peace. It was a metal keepsake, not a living plant.
The NASA photograph below shows the object before the flight. The floating illustration is a symbolic drawing, not a photograph of the lunar surface.

disc.title: Messages from planet Earth
disc.intro: Many voices travelled together on one tiny disc.
paragraphs: The silicon disc carried goodwill messages from leaders of 73 countries, along with other records. Very small etched writing let these messages fit on its surface.
This preflight NASA photograph includes a coin for scale. The coin is not being identified as an object left on the Moon.

legacy.title: The story keeps going
legacy.intro: A mission can end while its questions live on.
paragraphs: The crew returned, Eagle's lower stage stayed, and samples reached Earth. Instruments, pictures and measurements helped people ask new questions about the Moon.
Try three discoveries. There is no timer, and you can always try again.

quiz.question: Which part of Eagle stayed on the Moon?
choices: The crew cabin with the astronauts
quiz.explanation: The lower stage became the launch platform. The upper stage lifted the astronauts back to lunar orbit.

quiz.question: Where is the laser used for lunar ranging?
choices: Inside a battery on the Moon
quiz.explanation: The Earth-based laser sends light to a passive reflector on the Moon.

quiz.question: Which kind of evidence can travel home?
quiz.explanation: The returned samples let laboratories study real lunar material.

sojourner-preview.title: Sojourner · 1997
sojourner-preview.intro: Little wheels. A new way to explore.
paragraphs: Pathfinder brought Sojourner to Mars in 1997. Open the 1997 mission monitor to explore its interactive archive.

about.title: Small objects. Extraordinary stories.
about.intro: Look closer at what exploration leaves behind.
paragraphs: Explore a mission, open an object and follow its evidence back to NASA. Scientific photographs stay separate from our illustrated archive setting.

The rooms and decorative artwork are AI-generated illustrations, not photographs of a historical control room. NASA does not endorse this project. Apollo and Viking include owner-provided illustrated arrival animations. Narration recordings are credited separately.

help.title: Your explorer's guide
help.intro: Follow your curiosity. Take your time.
paragraphs: Choose Apollo 11, Viking 1 or Sojourner. Explore archive takes you straight to the room; Watch the story plays the illustrated journey and narrated welcome. The Objects menu lists the exhibits.
Use Tab to move between controls and Enter to open one. Press Escape to close a page. Every evidence image has a credit and a source. You can pause decorative motion at any time.

Use the Field guide to find evidence and complete three learning goals in each mission. Objects opened and learning goals are counted separately. Progress is saved on this device when browser storage is available.

art-info.title: How this archive was made
art-info.intro: AI-generated illustrations, films, narration and music. Original NASA evidence is credited separately.
paragraphs: AI tools helped create the illustrative setting, films, narrator voices, music, code and explanatory text. These creative elements are separate from original NASA evidence.

Illustrations and imagined character portraits are not historical photographs. Narrator stories are modern educational explanations, not original mission transmissions. The cassette’s NASA/JPL archive excerpts are credited separately.
The smiling explorer guides are imagined navigation helpers. Their tips explain how to use this archive; they are not historical spacecraft messages.

apollo-story.title: Eagle’s Journey to the Moon
apollo-story.intro: A short narrated story based on NASA sources. Not an original mission transmission.
paragraphs: Hello, explorer! Ready for a journey to the Moon?
Meet Eagle, Apollo Eleven’s lunar module. In July nineteen sixty-nine, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin flew Eagle down to the Moon. Michael Collins stayed in orbit, ready for their return.
Eagle had no wheels. It landed on four legs! The astronauts explored on foot, collected Moon rocks, and set up experiments.
When it was time to leave, Eagle’s upper cabin lifted off. Its lower stage stayed behind, serving as a launch platform.
And the story didn’t stop there. A special reflector left on the Moon still helps scientists measure the distance from Earth.
Some equipment stayed, but its story kept going.
Now it’s your turn. Look at the photographs, open the files, and follow the clues. What will you discover?

crt-intro-text.title: Welcome to the Apollo Eleven archive
crt-intro-text.intro: An original NASA-based introduction, not a historic transmission.
paragraphs: The year is nineteen sixty-nine. Eagle has landed on the Moon.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin have arrived in a spacecraft with two stages. The upper cabin will take them back into lunar orbit. The lower stage will stay behind.
But leaving equipment behind does not mean leaving its story behind.
Welcome to the Apollo Eleven archive.
Tap a screen to meet Eagle. Open the photographs to discover real NASA evidence. Pick up a file, explore an experiment, or answer a question in the notebook.
Each object holds a clue to how people reached the Moon—and what they left there.
Look closely, explorer. Your mission starts now.

viking-mission.title: A new chapter on Mars
viking-mission.intro: A robot explorer, an orbiter and a new world.
paragraphs: Viking 1 launched on August 20, 1975. It reached Mars orbit on June 19, 1976. The lander touched down on July 20.
The orbiter stayed above Mars while the lander worked on the ground. Each had a different job.

viking-lander.title: Meet Viking 1
viking-lander.intro: A science station that stayed in one place.
paragraphs: Viking 1 was a lander, not a rover. It explored its surroundings with cameras, a sampling arm and scientific instruments.
Explore NASA’s original Viking lander model. Drag to rotate or use the controls to zoom. Display colors and lighting have been adjusted for clarity; use Original model colors to compare.

viking-weather.title: A weather station on Mars
viking-weather.intro: Even a still explorer can watch a planet change.
paragraphs: Viking measured temperature, pressure and wind. This chart shows its daily average air pressure for Mars days 1–30 after landing.
A Mars day is called a sol. Each plotted point comes from the archived VL1 table; the connecting lines do not add new measurements.
The archive includes warning flags about data coverage. Open the table to see the values and flags alongside the graph.

viking-photos.title: The first view from the ground
viking-photos.intro: Rocks, dust—and a piece of the explorer itself.
paragraphs: Look at the right side: part of Viking’s footpad appears in the first surface photograph. Nearby, its camera saw rocks and fine-grained material.
A small detail can tell a big story. This image is evidence from Mars, not a drawing.
viking-photos.question: Can you find the footpad? What does the photograph show clearly?

viking-color.title: Mars in color
viking-color.intro: A closer look at a rocky world.
paragraphs: This is NASA’s first color image from Viking Lander 1. Compare it with the black-and-white view.
The original NASA file is preserved. The small print on the desk is a preview; this panel shows the full image.

viking-panorama.title: Look a little further
viking-panorama.intro: A wider view of the landing site.
paragraphs: A panorama brings a broad stretch of the surroundings into one image. Follow the horizon and look for changes in the rocky ground.

viking-soil.title: Big questions in a little soil
viking-soil.intro: Could Mars hold signs of life?
paragraphs: Viking’s biology experiments tested Martian soil. The results revealed puzzling chemical activity, but did not provide clear evidence of living microorganisms.
An exciting signal is a reason to investigate carefully. It is not enough to announce that life has been found.

viking-timeline.title: From launch to a lasting archive
viking-timeline.intro: Different dates tell different parts of the story.
paragraphs: 20 August 1975: launch. 19 June 1976: Mars orbit. 20 July 1976: surface landing.
The lander stopped operating on November 11, 1982 after a faulty command. The lander and orbiter had separate operating histories.

viking-message.title: Pictures that called home
viking-message.intro: A short narrated story based on NASA sources. Not an original mission transmission.
paragraphs: Hello, explorer! Ready for a visit to Mars?
Meet Viking One. In July nineteen seventy-six, this robotic lander touched down on the Red Planet. No astronauts were aboard.
Viking had no wheels—just three landing legs! It stayed in one place and explored the ground around it.
Its cameras revealed rocks and dust. Its instruments measured the Martian weather, and a long arm collected soil.
Some experiments searched for signs of life. The results were puzzling, but they did not clearly prove that living things were there.
Viking One sent its final message home in nineteen eighty-two. Its radio grew quiet, but its photographs and measurements are still here to explore.
Now it’s your turn. Open the photographs, follow the weather record, and try the notebook quiz. What will you discover?
viking-message.illustrationAlt: An imagined friendly Viking lander on three legs on an illustrated Martian plain, saying Hello, explorer!
viking-message.illustrationCaption: An imagined Viking character. A story grounded in NASA facts.

viking-legacy.title: Quiet hardware, lasting discoveries
viking-legacy.intro: The explorer stopped. The questions continued.
paragraphs: Viking 1’s final transmission reached Earth on November 11, 1982. Its photographs and measurements remain available to explore.
Try these three questions, then return to the archive and follow another clue.

quiz.question: How did Viking 1 explore Mars?
choices: It worked from a fixed landing site.
quiz.explanation: Viking was a stationary robotic lander, with cameras and instruments.

quiz.question: What does the green chart show?
quiz.explanation: The chart uses archived Viking 1 pressure measurements in millibars.

quiz.question: Did the biology tests clearly prove life existed?
choices: Yes, a picture showed a living creature.
No; the results did not give clear evidence of living microorganisms.
quiz.explanation: Interesting chemical activity needs careful interpretation and more evidence.

viking-crt-intro-text.title: Welcome to the Viking One archive
viking-crt-intro-text.intro: Original NASA-based explanatory narration, not historic radio audio.
paragraphs: The year is nineteen seventy-six. Viking One has arrived on Mars.
No astronauts are aboard. This robotic lander has touched down on Chryse Planitia, a wide Martian plain.
Its cameras reveal rocks and dust. Its instruments study the weather, and its sampling arm gathers soil for experiments.
Viking One will stay at its landing site. Its job is to look closely, measure carefully, and send discoveries home.
Welcome to the Viking One archive.
Tap a screen to meet the lander. Compare the real NASA photographs, open the mission file, and explore the weather record.
See the glowing question mark? Open the notebook and try the discovery quiz.
Look closely, explorer. Your Mars mission starts now.

sojourner-mission.title: A small rover, a long journey
sojourner-mission.intro: Choose a moment. Follow the evidence.
paragraphs: Pathfinder carried Sojourner to Mars. One stayed at the landing site; the other could move to nearby rocks.
The dates below mark different events: launch, landing, rover deployment and the final data received from Pathfinder.

sojourner-rover.title: Meet Sojourner & Pathfinder
sojourner-rover.intro: A mobile rover and its landing partner. Turn them around and look closer.
paragraphs: Choose the Sojourner rover or the Pathfinder lander in the 3D viewer. Both models are educational reconstructions created for this project using NASA diagrams and hardware photographs. They are not NASA-issued model files or engineering CAD.
The original NASA photograph below shows the real Sojourner rover near Barnacle Bill, taken by the Pathfinder lander. Use it to compare historical evidence with the simplified model.

sojourner-duration.title: Beyond the plan
sojourner-duration.intro: What can seven and eighty-three tell us?
paragraphs: NASA reports a seven-day planned rover mission and 83 days of Sojourner operation. These bars compare those two summary values.
They are days, not Martian sols, a daily activity record or a series of sensor measurements. A longer bar means a longer reported duration.

sojourner-photos.title: Ready to roll
sojourner-photos.intro: Before the little wheels touched the ground.
paragraphs: Pathfinder took this early picture after landing. Sojourner is still on the lander; the white material nearby belongs to the deflated airbags.
Notice the difference between the rover, the lander and the landscape. They are three different parts of this picture.

sojourner-barnacle.title: A rock called Barnacle Bill
sojourner-barnacle.intro: A closer look, one rock at a time.
paragraphs: The lander camera recorded this view on sol 3. The rover later moved into position to examine Barnacle Bill with its rear-mounted APXS instrument.
The instrument is not visible in this photograph. A photo and an instrument reading give us different kinds of evidence.

sojourner-yogi.title: A rover-eye view of Yogi
sojourner-yogi.intro: This time, the camera traveled with the rover.
paragraphs: Sojourner used its rear color camera for this close view of Yogi. The image record is dated July 11, 1997.
Compare it with the lander photographs. The camera location changes what we can see.

sojourner-landing.title: A landing with a soft bounce
sojourner-landing.intro: How do you protect a rover on arrival?
paragraphs: A parachute slowed Pathfinder during descent. Airbags cushioned the landing before opening the way for the rover.
On sol 2, Sojourner rolled down a ramp and onto Mars. The lander remained its partner for communications.

sojourner-timeline.title: Two dates, different meanings
sojourner-timeline.intro: Last contact is different from formal mission termination.
paragraphs: NASA received the final Pathfinder data on September 27, 1997. The team continued trying to restore communications.
A NASA Photojournal note gives March 10, 1998 as formal mission termination. The mission overview lists September 27, 1997 as its end date; this archive labels both events separately.

sojourner-message.title: A little rover and its big adventure
sojourner-message.intro: Meet a little rover with six wheels and a big adventure.
paragraphs: Hello, explorer! Meet Sojourner, a little rover with six wheels and a big adventure.
In nineteen ninety-seven, Pathfinder carried it all the way to Mars. Airbags cushioned their landing. Then Sojourner rolled down a ramp and onto the rocky ground.
Its solar panel helped provide power. Its cameras took pictures, and an instrument checked what rocks and soil were made of.
Sojourner and Pathfinder were a team. The rover explored nearby, while the lander helped its discoveries reach Earth.
Their radio signals are quiet now, but their pictures and discoveries are still here.
Look closely, little explorer. What clues will you find?
sojourner-message.illustrationAlt: Imagined smiling Sojourner character on Mars saying Hello, explorer; decorative story illustration.
sojourner-message.illustrationCaption: An imagined guide, not a NASA photograph. Story based on linked NASA records.

sojourner-cassette.title: Listen to the mission archive
sojourner-cassette.intro: Choose a chapter. Hear the voices and read along.
paragraphs: These excerpts come from NASA/JPL’s 2022 podcast First Steps: Sojourner. Modern narration and interviews are labeled separately from the 1997 mission-control excerpt.
The cassette is an illustrated archive prop. These are edited NASA/JPL recordings, not Sojourner speaking or sounds recorded by a microphone on Mars.

sojourner-solar.title: Sunlight for a little rover
sojourner-solar.intro: The panel on top helped power exploration.
paragraphs: Sojourner used solar power and batteries. Its solar panel helped turn sunlight into electrical energy.
Use the educational model to locate the solar array, then compare it with the original NASA hardware photograph. The small cell pattern and materials are simplified.

sojourner-relay.title: A team across space
paragraphs: Sojourner communicated through the Pathfinder lander. The two vehicles had different jobs: one explored nearby ground; the other acted as a link with Earth.
A rover camera and a lander camera can show the same place from very different viewpoints.

sojourner-legacy.title: What did we discover?
sojourner-legacy.intro: Keep asking questions after the signals fall silent.
paragraphs: Sojourner demonstrated mobile exploration on Mars. Its pictures and rock investigations became part of a lasting scientific record.
The rover remains on Mars. Its historical work continues through the evidence we can study today.

quiz.question: Which vehicle could move across the ground?
quiz.explanation: Sojourner was the rover. Pathfinder was the lander and communications partner.

quiz.question: What do 7 and 83 compare here?
choices: Planned and reported rover operation in days
quiz.explanation: These are NASA mission-summary durations in days, not sols or a weather record.

quiz.question: Who took the close-up color image of Yogi?
quiz.explanation: NASA identifies the camera as Sojourner’s rear color camera.

sojourner-crt-intro-text.title: Sojourner - arrival record
sojourner-crt-intro-text.intro: The readable version of the CRT welcome. Modern NASA-based narration, not historical radio audio.
paragraphs: The year is nineteen ninety-seven. Pathfinder has landed on Mars, carrying a small rover named Sojourner.
The landing place is Ares Vallis, an ancient floodplain filled with rocks.
Pathfinder stays in place. On the second Martian day, Sojourner rolls down a ramp and begins exploring on six little wheels.
Together, their cameras and instruments help people study this new world.
Welcome to the Sojourner archive.
Tap the middle screen to turn the educational three-dimensional models. Open the landing file and compare real NASA photographs.
Tap the cassette to hear NASA voices. See the glowing question mark? Open the notebook and try the discovery quiz.
Your little Mars adventure starts now.

apollo.name: Launch from Earth
apollo.description: Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins launch together on Apollo 11. Their goal: land people on the Moon and bring them home.

apollo.name: Eagle lands
apollo.description: Armstrong and Aldrin land in Eagle at the Sea of Tranquility. Collins remains in lunar orbit.
apollo.caption: AS11-40-5961 · NASA / Neil Armstrong. Eagle during the moonwalk, not a photograph of touchdown.

apollo.name: First step
apollo.description: Armstrong takes the first human step on the Moon. In the eastern United States it is still July 20. Dates depend on the time zone.

apollo.name: Safe return
apollo.description: All three astronauts return to Earth. Eagle’s lower stage remains on the Moon, while lunar samples come home with the crew.

viking.name: Launch from Earth

viking.description: Viking 1 enters orbit around Mars. Images from above help the team examine possible landing places.

viking.name: Surface landing
viking.description: The lander touches down at Chryse Planitia. The orbiter continues working above Mars.

viking.name: The first picture
viking.description: Viking 1 returns its first surface photograph. Rocks, fine material and part of its footpad appear in the image.

sojourner.description: Pathfinder launches carrying the small Sojourner rover.

sojourner.description: Pathfinder lands at Ares Vallis with protective airbags. Sojourner is still on the lander.

sojourner.name: Rover deployment
sojourner.description: Sojourner rolls down the ramp onto the surface. A sol is a Martian day.

sojourner.name: Final data received
sojourner.description: The final Pathfinder data arrive on Earth. Attempts to restore communication continue afterward.

crtIntro.label: SOJOURNER / ARRIVAL RECORD / 04 JUL 1997
paragraphs: The year is nineteen ninety-seven. Pathfinder has landed on Mars, carrying a small rover named Sojourner.
The landing place is Ares Vallis, an ancient floodplain filled with rocks.
Pathfinder stays in place. On the second Martian day, Sojourner rolls down a ramp and begins exploring on six little wheels.
Together, their cameras and instruments help people study this new world.
Welcome to the Sojourner archive.
Tap the middle screen to turn the educational three-dimensional models. Open the landing file and compare real NASA photographs.
Tap the cassette to hear NASA voices. See the glowing question mark? Open the notebook and try the discovery quiz.
Your little Mars adventure starts now.

audio.alignment: Local speech-recognition word estimates aligned to the approved NASA-based script. Spoken year normalized; Ares Vallis spelling retained from NASA sources. Playback follows audio.currentTime, including pauses and seeking. Editorial word timings, not historical mission timestamps.
